source_text: καὶ μήτε καταθρασυνομένους αὐθάδως τῶν πλουσίων κλητῶν μήτε αὖ πάλιν ὑποπίπτοντας αὐτοῖς διὰ οἰκείαν φιλοκέρδειαν, πρῶτον μὲν αὐτῶν ἐξαιρεῖν τῷ λόγῳ τὴν κενὴν ἀπόγνωσιν καὶ δηλοῦν μετὰ τῆς δεούσης ἐξηγήσεως τῶν λογίων τοῦ κυρίου διότι οὐκ ἀποκέκοπται τέλεον αὐτοῖς ἡ κληρονομία τῆς βασιλείας τῶν οὐρανῶν, ἐὰν ὑπακούσωσι ταῖς ἐντολαῖς· εἶθ᾿ ὁπόταν μάθωσιν ὡς ἀδεὲς δεδίασι δέος καὶ ὅτι βουλομένους αὐτοὺς ὁ σωτὴρ ἀσμένως δέχεται, τότε καὶ προδεικνύναι καὶ μυσταγωγεῖν, ὅπως ἂν καὶ δι᾿ οἵων ἔργων τε καὶ διαθέσεων ἐπαύραιντο τῆς ἐλπίδος, ὡς οὔτ᾿ ἀμηχάνου καθεστώσης αὐτοῖς οὔτε τοὐναντίον εἰκῇ περιγινομένης. ἀλλ᾿ ὅνπερ τρόπον ἔχει τὸ τῶν ἀθλητῶν, ἵνα μικρὰ καὶ ἐπίκηρα μεγάλοις καὶ ἀφθάρτοις παραβάλωμεν, τουτὶ καὶ ἐφ᾿ ἑαυτοῦ ὁ κατὰ κόσμον πλουτῶν λογιζέσθω. καὶ γὰρ ἐκείνων ὁ μὲν ὅτι δυνήσεται νικᾶν καὶ στεφάνων τυγχάνειν ἀπελπίσας οὐδ᾿ ὅλως ἐπὶ τὴν ἄθλησιν ἀπεγράψατο. ὁ δὲ ταύτην μὲν ἐμβαλόμενος τῇ γνώμῃ τὴν ἐλπίδα, πόνους δὲ καὶ γυμνάσια καὶ τροφὰς μὴ προσιέμενος προσφόρους, ἀστεφάνωτος διεγένετο καὶ διήμαρτε τῶν ἐλπίδων. οὕτως τις καὶ τὴν ἐπίγειον ταύτην περιβεβλημένος περιβολὴν μήτε τὴν ἀρχὴν ἑαυτὸν τῶν ἄθλων τοῦ σωτῆρος ἐκκηρυσσέτω, πιστός γε ὢν καὶ τὸ μεγαλεῖον συνορῶν τῆς τοῦ θεοῦ φιλανθρωπίας, μήτε μὴν αὖθις ἀνάσκητος καὶ ἀναγώνιστος μείνας ἀκονιτὶ κἀνιδρωτὶ τῶν στεφάνων τῆς ἀφθαρσίας ἐλπιζέτω μεταλαβεῖν· ἀλλ᾿ αὑτὸν ὑποβαλέτω φέρων γυμναστῇ μὲν τῶ λόγῳ. ἀγωνοθέτῃ δὲ τῷ Χριστῷ· τροφὴ δὲ αὐτῷ καὶ ποτὸν γενέσθω τεταγμένον ἡ καινὴ διαθήκη τοῦ κυρίου. γυμνάσια δὲ αἱ ἐντολαί. εὐσχημοσύνη δὲ καὶ κόσμος αἱ καλαὶ διαθέσεις, ἀγάπη, πίστις. ἐλπίς, γνῶσις ἀληθείας . . . . . . . . . . . . . πραότης, εὐσπλαγχνία, σεμνότης, ἵν᾿, ὅταν ἡ ἐσχάτη σάλπιγξ ὑποσημήνῃ τοῦ δρόμου καὶ τῆς ἐντεῦθεν ἐξόδου καθάπερ ἐκ σταδίου τοῦ βίου, μετ᾿ ἀγαθοῦ τοῦ συνειδότος τῷ ἀθλοθέτῃ παραστῇ νικηφόρος, ὡμολογημένος τῆς ἄνω πατρίδος ἄξιος, εἰς ἣν μετὰ στεφάνων καὶ κηρυγμάτων ἀγγελικῶν ἐπανέρχεται.
thought_title: The rich must train like athletes for the heavenly contest
orientation: Clement is addressing how teachers should deal with rich believers who have heard the Gospel's hard sayings about wealth.
pass_a_gloss: and neither being bold against the rich called ones in a self-willed way nor again falling down before them because of their own love of gain, first to take away from them by the word the empty despair and to show with the necessary explanation of the sayings of the Lord that the inheritance of the kingdom of heaven has not been cut off from them completely, if they obey the commandments; then whenever they learn that they have feared a fear without cause and that the Savior receives them gladly when they are willing, then also to show beforehand and to initiate them, how and through what works and dispositions they may enjoy the hope, since it is neither impossible for them nor on the contrary comes about for them at random. But just as the matter of athletes is, in order that we may compare small and perishable things with great and imperishable things, let the one who is rich according to the world consider this also in his own case. For also of those, the one who despaired that he would be able to win and obtain crowns did not at all enroll for the contest. But the one who cast this hope into his mind, but did not accept toils and exercises and suitable foods, remained uncrowned and missed the hopes. So let not someone who has put on this earthly garment proclaim himself out of the contests of the Savior from the beginning, if he is faithful and sees together the greatness of God's love for humanity, nor again let him, remaining untrained and uncontested, hope to share in the crowns of incorruption without dust and without sweat; but let him submit himself, bringing himself to the word as trainer, and to Christ as judge of the contest; and let the new covenant of the Lord be appointed food and drink for him. And let the commandments be exercises. And let good dispositions be seemliness and adornment, love, faith, hope, knowledge of truth, gentleness, compassion, dignity, in order that, whenever the last trumpet signals the race and the departure from here as from the stadium of life, he may stand beside the judge of the contest with a good conscience as victor, acknowledged worthy of the fatherland above, into which he returns with crowns and angelic proclamations.

choices.why: The participle form refers to those who have been called by God; 'called ones' preserves the passive sense and avoids the interpretive 'the called' as a fixed class.
The phrase is deliberately paradoxical (a fear that is not fearful); rendering it literally keeps Clement's wordplay visible.
The two adverbs are technical athletic terms for winning without contest; keeping both as separate adverbial phrases preserves the vivid image.
The dative with γυμναστῇ is instrumental; 'to the word as trainer' keeps the metaphor of submitting oneself to a trainer while preserving the dative force.

choices.english: and to Christ as judge of the contest
choices.why: ἀγωνοθέτης is the official who presides over and judges the games; 'judge of the contest' captures the role better than 'umpire' or 'president'.
The phrase echoes 1 Corinthians 15:52; keeping 'last trumpet' preserves the biblical resonance.

bible_refs.note: The athletic imagery of running, training, and receiving crowns echoes Paul's comparison of the Christian life to athletic contests.
The phrase 'the last trumpet' (ἡ ἐσχάτη σάλπιγξ) recalls Paul's description of the resurrection at the last trumpet.

pass_b_english: They must neither be bold and insolent toward the rich who have been called, nor again fall down before them out of their own love of gain. First, by the word they must take away their empty despair and show, with the necessary explanation of the Lord's sayings, that the inheritance of the kingdom of heaven has not been cut off from them completely, if they obey the commandments. Then, when they learn that what they fear is a fear without cause and that the Savior gladly receives them when they are willing, they must also point out beforehand and initiate them into how and through what works and dispositions they may enjoy the hope, since it is neither impossible for them nor, on the contrary, something that comes to them without effort.

But just as it is with athletes, to compare small and perishable things with great and imperishable ones, let the person who is rich according to the world reason in the same way about himself. For among those athletes, the one who despairs that he will be able to win and obtain crowns does not enroll in the contest at all. But the one who places this hope in his mind, yet does not accept the labors and exercises and suitable food, remains uncrowned and fails in his hopes. So also let the one who has put on this earthly garment not proclaim himself excluded from the Savior's contests from the start, if he is faithful and perceives the greatness of God's love for humanity; nor again let him remain untrained and uncontested and hope to receive the crowns of incorruption without dust and without sweat. Rather, let him submit himself, bearing it, to the word as trainer and to Christ as judge of the contest. Let his appointed food and drink be the new covenant of the Lord, and the commandments his exercises. Let his seemliness and adornment be the good dispositions: love, faith, hope, knowledge of truth, gentleness, compassion, dignity, so that when the last trumpet signals the end of the race and the departure from here, as from the stadium of life, he may stand before the judge of the contest with a good conscience as victor, acknowledged as worthy of the fatherland above, into which he returns with crowns and angelic proclamations.

last_rejected.why: Greek says “empty ignorance”, not “despair”. Changes meaning.
Greek refers to “without spear and without blood”, not dust or sweat.
last_rejected.ruling: ἀκονιτί = 'without dust' (κόνις), ἰδρόω = 'sweat'; standard athletic idiom for effortless victory.
